posts.title: Cities in literature
posts.description: Needless to say, this is not just a list of books that happen to be set in one city or another; that would be of little use, and I would not even know how to begin researching a topic of this breadth. My goal, rather, was to compile a reasonably conservative canon of “literature of the city”: that is, those works that approach urban locations as one of their central themes, attempting to show what cities are like , and what it means or how it feels to live in them. A wearisome cliché used to describe many books featured below is that within their pages “the city becomes its own character”. The specificity of location is certainly the most widely recognizable feature of city literature: a traditional “urban novel” carefully follows a clear topography and abounds in detailed descriptions of different streets, neighborhoods, landmarks, and various locales. posts.title: Strange, fantastic, and futuristic cities in fiction
posts.description: This list of literary works set in imaginary or speculative cities not only complements my list of more mainstream urban literature , but was researched concurrently with it, and in fact, my initial goal was to publish just one long list of city books without discriminating between genres or typical library sections. Following Baudelaire and Eliot , I wanted to argue that any urban space can be experienced – and depicted in writing – as “unreal”: essentially mysterious, dreamlike (or indeed nightmarish), and spellbinding, and that all books about cities therefore deserved a place on a single, sprawling map. The sheer number of titles I ended up amassing was one reason I decided to make the “real/unreal” split after all; another was the realization that such a clear distinction would simply be more useful for the majority of my audience than the rather abstract point I was planning to make. posts.title: Spy and secret agent comics
posts.description: “Spy fiction” designates such a broad array of works that it is almost useless as a descriptive label. The only thing it can reliably promise is that a given story will feature at least one character engaged in clandestine work for some shadowy organization with at least notional governmental backing. But the narrative itself may range from a lighthearted, action-packed adventure in a world of double-crossing lovers, exotic locales, luxury cars, and hi-tech gadgets to a miserable and decidedly unglamorous affair full of tired, disaffected people troubled by second thoughts about the moral aspects of their service that never ceases to demand of them still more and more sacrifices. One would expect that comic books, because of their general association with the pulpy side of popular culture, would feature almost exclusively espionage stories of the first kind, complete with sexually irresistible and physically invulnerable martini-drinking main characters.
